cores.title: From actions to pull counts
assumptions: K is a positive finite number of arms; means are fixed real numbers.
An arbitrary action sequence is observed for a finite horizon T.
cores.question: Let Δ_i=max_j μ_j−μ_i and N_i(T) count the choices of arm i. Derive the gap-weighted pull-count identity for pseudo-regret. Does the identity require independent rewards or a causal policy?
cores.answer: R_T=T μ_*−Σ_{t<T} μ_{A_t}=Σ_{t<T}(μ_*−μ_{A_t})=Σ_i Δ_i N_i(T). Partition the finite time set by the chosen arm. This is a deterministic identity for any action trace; no reward law, independence or policy causality is used. It alone provides no useful bound on N_i(T), realized reward fluctuations or regret rate.
rubric: Expand the finite time sum correctly.
Group each time exactly once by its chosen arm.
Separate deterministic accounting from statistical or causal assumptions and from a rate theorem.

cores.title: When may expectation cross the sum?
assumptions: Fix finite arm means μ_i∈ℝ and finite horizon T; Δ_i=μ_*−μ_i and pathwise pseudo-regret is R_T=Σ_i Δ_i N_i(T).
A measure space, finite arm set and random action trace are fixed.
For every arm, its real-valued finite-horizon pull count is integrable.
cores.question: Derive the expected pseudo-regret decomposition from its pathwise version. Identify the analytic condition needed, and explain whether the conclusion is a realized-regret concentration bound.
cores.answer: Each gap is a constant, so its product with an integrable pull count is integrable. The finite sum is integrable, expectation commutes with this sum, and constants factor out: E[R_T]=Σ_i Δ_i E[N_i(T)]. This is an integral identity under the stated integrability premises, not a tail bound for realized rewards. Reward noise needs separate analysis. The abstract library theorem even permits a general measure; probability semantics require choosing a probability measure.
rubric: Apply finite-sum integral linearity and constant multiplication.
Do not infer a tail bound, independent samples or probability-space semantics from a general measure identity.

cores.title: An infinite confidence budget
assumptions: Bad events B_n, n≥0, satisfy P(B_n)≤δ/2^(n+1) under the same probability law.
cores.question: Bound the probability that any B_n occurs. Is event independence needed? Distinguish the deterministic budget calculation from the statistical guarantee that supplies each event bound.
cores.answer: Countable subadditivity gives P(∪_n B_n)≤Σ_n P(B_n)≤Σ_n δ/2^(n+1)=δ. Independence between the events is unnecessary. The geometric-series identity only allocates a budget; it does not prove P(B_n)≤δ/2^(n+1). For adaptive histories, the algorithm must supply applicable conditional bounds or unconditional event bounds for the actual process, not fixed-design statements silently applied after selection.
rubric: Use countable subadditivity under one law.
Sum the schedule from n=0 with correct normalization.
Reject a need for event independence and distinguish the missing statistical supplier.

cores.title: A confidence interval is not an unbiased estimate
assumptions: μ is a real mean and r>0.
An estimate satisfies |estimate−μ|≤r with probability one.
cores.question: Does this guarantee imply that estimate is unbiased? Give a counterexample. Does it imply that successive estimation errors are independent?
cores.answer: No. The deterministic estimate μ+r/2 has error r/2≤r with probability one but expectation μ+r/2, hence nonzero bias. This is a logical countermodel, not an implementable estimator when μ is unknown. To refute independence, reuse the same fair random sign S∈{−1,1} at two times and set both errors to r S/2. Both estimates satisfy the interval and are unbiased, but P(error_1>0,error_2>0)=1/2≠1/4. Neither unbiasedness nor independence follows from interval coverage.
rubric: Exhibit a positive-radius counterexample and compute its bias.
Give a joint law violating independence while preserving both intervals.
Explain that an analysis countermodel need not be an executable unknown-mean procedure.
